cards.front: An {{c1::allele}} is one version of a gene.
cards.quote: An allele is one version of a gene.
cards.section: Explain: alleles can hide but do not disappear

cards.front: A {{c1::dominant}} allele shows its trait even when there is only one copy.
cards.quote: A dominant allele shows its trait even when there is only one copy.
cards.section: Explain: alleles can hide but do not disappear

cards.front: A recessive allele shows its trait only when {{c1::both copies}} are recessive.
cards.quote: A recessive allele shows its trait only when both copies are recessive.
cards.section: Explain: alleles can hide but do not disappear

cards.front: For a pea plant with the genotype Pp, what is its genotype, and what is its phenotype?
cards.back: The genotype is the pair of alleles, Pp. The phenotype is the trait that shows, purple flowers.
cards.quote: Your genotype is the pair of alleles you carry, such as Pp. Your phenotype is the trait that shows, such as purple flowers.
cards.section: Explain: alleles can hide but do not disappear

cards.front: In the one-gene pea model, a Pp plant has purple flowers. What happens to its white allele, p?
cards.back: It is hidden, not destroyed. The dominant P masks it, but the plant still carries p and can pass it on.
cards.quote: A dominant allele masks a recessive one: it hides it from view without destroying it.
cards.section: Explain: alleles can hide but do not disappear

cards.front: A Pp pea plant makes sex cells. What allele does each sex cell carry, and with what chance?
cards.back: Each sex cell carries only one allele: P with a 50 percent chance or p with a 50 percent chance.
cards.quote: A Pp plant passes on P or p, with a 50 percent chance for each.
cards.section: Explain: alleles can hide but do not disappear

cards.front: A PP pea plant is crossed with a pp pea plant. What is the genotype and flower color of every offspring?
cards.back: Every offspring is Pp and purple. The PP parent can only pass P and the pp parent can only pass p.
cards.why: Each offspring carries a hidden p.
cards.quote: A PP plant can only pass on P. A pp plant can only pass on p.
cards.section: Explain: alleles can hide but do not disappear

cards.front: {{c1::Probability}} is the chance that something will happen.
cards.quote: Probability is the chance that something will happen.
cards.section: Explain: a Punnett square shows the chances

cards.front: In a Punnett square for two Pp parents, what is the chance of one particular box, and how do you get it?
cards.back: 1/4. Each parent gives the needed allele with a 1 in 2 chance, so 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
cards.quote: Each allele has a 1 in 2 chance. So every box has the same chance: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
cards.section: Explain: a Punnett square shows the chances

cards.front: Two Pp pea plants are crossed. Give the genotype chances and the phenotype ratio of the offspring.
cards.back: 1/4 PP, 2/4 Pp, 1/4 pp. Phenotypes: 3 purple to 1 white.
cards.why: PP and Pp are both purple.
cards.quote: One box is PP, two are Pp and one is pp, so the genotype chances are 1/4 PP, 2/4 Pp and 1/4 pp.
cards.section: Explain: a Punnett square shows the chances

cards.front: What parent genotypes does the 3 purple : 1 white prediction need?
cards.back: Two Pp parents (one gene, one dominant allele, known parent genotypes).
cards.quote: This 3 : 1 prediction needs two Pp parents.
cards.section: Explain: a Punnett square shows the chances

cards.front: A Pp plant is crossed with a pp plant. What share of the offspring are predicted to be white?
cards.back: 1/2, or 50 percent. The pp parent always passes p. The Pp parent passes P or p, so half the boxes are Pp and half are pp.
cards.quote: The pp parent passes p. The Pp parent passes P or p. Half the boxes are Pp and half are pp.
cards.section: Explain: a Punnett square shows the chances

cards.front: A PP plant is crossed with a Pp plant. Can any offspring have white flowers? Why?
cards.back: No. The PP parent always passes P, so every offspring is purple. Some carry a hidden p.
cards.quote: The PP parent always passes P, so every offspring gets at least one P and is purple.
cards.section: Explore: breed purple and white pea plants

cards.front: In the one-gene model, two purple pea plants have a white-flowered offspring. What must both parents' genotypes be, and what is the chance the next offspring is white?
cards.back: Both parents are Pp. The next offspring has a 1 in 4 chance of being white.
cards.why: A white offspring needs p from each parent, so each parent had to carry p. A purple parent that carries p is Pp.
cards.quote: Two purple parents give white offspring only when both are Pp.
cards.section: Explore: breed purple and white pea plants

cards.front: Two Pp plants produce 4 offspring and all 4 are purple. Does this show the Punnett square is wrong?
cards.back: No. A Punnett square predicts chances, not exact counts. All purple in a group of 4 happens about 32 percent of the time.
cards.quote: Four seeds from two Pp parents might all bloom purple; the chance is about 32 percent.
cards.section: Explain: a Punnett square shows the chances

cards.front: Mendel crossed pea plants that differed in one trait. What did he see in the first offspring, and what did he do next to get his counts?
cards.back: The first offspring all showed the dominant trait. He let those hybrids fertilize themselves and counted the next generation.
cards.quote: He let those hybrids fertilize themselves and counted the next generation.
cards.section: Elaborate: Mendel’s pea counts

cards.front: Mendel counted 6,022 yellow and 2,001 green seeds from hybrid plants. What is the ratio of yellow to green, to two decimal places?
cards.back: 6,022 ÷ 2,001 is about 3.01, so about 3.01 : 1, very close to 3 : 1.
cards.quote: Divide the dominant count by the recessive count and round to two decimal places.
cards.section: Elaborate: Mendel’s pea counts

cards.front: Mendel counted 705 purple and 224 white flower plants. What percent were white, and how does it compare with the predicted percent?
cards.back: The total is 929, and 224 ÷ 929 is about 24 percent. The prediction is 25 percent, so it is close but not exact.
cards.quote: Divide 224 by the total, 929, and compare with 25 percent.
cards.section: Elaborate: Mendel’s pea counts

cards.front: A group has 3 dominant offspring for every 1 recessive offspring. Is the recessive share 1/3 or 1/4 of the total?
cards.back: 1/4. The total has four parts (3 + 1), and a fraction compares one group with the total.
cards.quote: A fraction compares one group with that total.
cards.section: Elaborate: Mendel’s pea counts

cards.front: Students cross two Pp plants in a simulation. Will a group of 1,000 offspring or a group of 4 offspring be likelier to land near 1 in 4 white? Why?
cards.back: The group of 1,000. Each offspring has a 1 in 4 chance, and small groups wander more.
cards.why: Real counts land near the predicted ratio but rarely match it exactly.
cards.quote: Your groups of 4 probably wandered from one in four.
cards.section: Explore: breed purple and white pea plants

cards.front: In the bead model of two Pp parents, why do you put both beads back after each draw?
cards.back: Parents do not run out of an allele after passing it on. Keeping beads out would change the chances after each draw.
cards.quote: Parents do not run out of an allele after passing it on, so replace both beads.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the bead model, a PP bag is paired with a Pp bag as a control. What result do you expect, and what does it check?
cards.back: It should never give a pp offspring. This checks that your method works.
cards.quote: It should never give a pp offspring, which checks that your method works.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a bead test of sample size, you make 4, 20 or 100 offspring from two Pp bags and record the percent that are pp. What result would show that sample size matters?
cards.back: The 100-offspring groups usually land closer to 25 percent than the 4-offspring groups.
cards.why: This rests on the rule that real counts come near the predicted chance but rarely match it exactly.
cards.quote: If the 100-offspring groups usually land closer to 25 percent than the 4-offspring groups, sample size matters.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Name one limit of the bead model of a pea cross.
cards.back: It is not a real plant. It has one gene and no weather, soil or lost seeds.
cards.quote: The bead model is not a real plant: it has one gene and no weather, soil or lost seeds.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A gardener crosses two Pp plants and grows 40 seeds. How many white plants should the gardener expect, and would 14 white plants show the prediction failed?
cards.back: Expect about 10 white (1/4 of 40). 14 would not show failure: the prediction gives chances, and small groups can vary from the predicted count.
cards.why: Rule: Punnett squares predict chances, not exact offspring counts.
cards.quote: For one-gene crosses, Punnett squares predict chances, not exact offspring counts.
cards.section: Explain: a Punnett square shows the chances
